# What we know

Ten findings drawn from five real runs (see [cases.md](cases.md)). Each says
where it comes from.

## 1. Variance comes from the brief, not from the model

Given the same brief, three models (Sonnet, Opus, Fable) returned almost the
same thing: a dark navigation instrument, a signage typeface. One model given
four briefs returned four really different proposals. Switching models,
raising the temperature or multiplying attempts does not buy diversity.
*Case 2.*

## 2. Precision about the problem opens, precision about the solution closes

The more you describe the use (who, where, in how many seconds, with which
hand), the more good answers there are. Naming the artefact ("a compass
rose", "a map", "a table") means the design decision has already been taken.
A human designer would ask "why a rose?". The model just executes. *Case 2.*

## 3. A cited reference becomes a target

Inspirations mentioned in passing were treated as a specification. Citing a
reference means ordering it. *Case 2.*

## 4. Asking for boldness produces nothing

The only device that worked: have the model write its default proposal, then
forbid it. In case 2, the answer discarded by the only agent that diverged
described exactly what the other three had produced. In cases 4 and 5, no
variant kept the skeleton of the defaults (tile grid, rounded cards, centred
clock). *Cases 2, 4, 5.*

## 5. A ban moves convergence, it does not remove it

With IBM Plex and cream backgrounds banned, everyone switched to the dark
instrument. Bans get you out of a rut, they do not open the field. *Case 2.*

## 6. Different angles, not opposites

An opposite mandate pushes the same slider to the other end: dark against
light, dense against sparse. Both answer the same question, they contradict
each other by construction, and you knew it before running them. A different
angle asks another question: "how do you read a station board while
walking?" against "how does a front page rank one big story?". Each one
shows what the others do not see. *Principle adopted in case
1, not measured.*

## 7. Skills set the floor, the model sets the ceiling

Sonnet, with a motion pack and written motion rules, delivered clean work on
the first attempt, with the best visual idea. It missed on judgement: a
reading rule broken, the signature line forgotten. Opus did the merge.
*Case 3.*

## 8. Blindness matters

A variant that sees the others drifts towards them. In case 3, the variant
that did not see the existing version is the one that brought the new idea.
*Case 3.*

## 9. The attractor shows in the defaults

The `default.md` files put side by side almost always describe the same
object. In cases 4 and 5: navy background, a single warm accent, a row of
rounded cards, a geometric grotesque, the same layout at every hour (8
defaults out of 8 in case 5). The agents say it themselves: "interchangeable
with any home-automation screen". It is the skill's best side product: at
last you know what bland looks like on this brief. *Cases 4, 5.*

## 10. What comes back unasked is the element most specific to the product

In case 2, three proposals out of four made, each on its own, the
disagreement between weather models their finest element. In case 4, all
five variants reorder the screen according to the time of day, though that
was the mandate of only one. In case 5, all eight variants hand the state
(alert, to do, calm) to a single object that changes nature. A convergence
that appears *between* different mandates is a signal to keep. *Cases 2, 4,
5.*

## What about the composition?

In case 2, the chosen direction was none of the proposals: it was an
assembly (the grid of one, the disc of another, "one hue per category" from
the third). Hence the composition step of the skill. But in cases 4 and 5, the composition
was rejected: too busy the first time, "created nothing" the second. The user
kept a single piece as it was, the rupture variant in case 4 and their own
pre-divergence version in case 5. Since then the composition is an option,
offered after the user has seen the variants, and it runs on Sonnet.
